imported_records.description: Studying matter, energy and their fundamental interactions.

concepts.label: James Webb Space Telescope
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why the infrared observatory must limit its own heat and how its shielding and position help.
concepts.card: The James Webb Space Telescope observes infrared light, so heat from its surroundings and its own structure can obscure faint signals. Its five separated sunshield layers reduce incoming heating, while an open design lets heat radiate into space.

evidence.note: Infrared thermal interference, five separated layers and radiative cooling.

relations.note: The source explains that the Sun–Earth L2 observing geometry lets Webb keep the Sun, Earth and Moon on the same shielded side.

concepts.label: Akashi Kaikyō Bridge
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why measured ground movement led to revised girder lengths during construction.
concepts.card: The Akashi Kaikyō Bridge’s construction encountered a geometry change in the 1995 earthquake. Its foundations moved with their supporting ground, changing the spacing between towers. Engineers revised the lengths of girders not yet fabricated, allowing work on the suspension bridge to continue.
concepts.original_description: suspension bridge in Kobe, Japan

evidence.locator: 1995 earthquake account, survey and girder revision
evidence.note: Foundation movement with ground and unfabricated girder-length adjustment.

relations.note: The operator identifies Akashi Kaikyō as a suspension bridge; its tower spacing and suspended girders make the earthquake-induced geometry change structurally consequential.

imported_records.description: suspension bridge in Kobe, Japan

concepts.label: Regenerative braking
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace energy from rotating wheels back into the traction battery during braking.
concepts.card: Regenerative braking makes a vehicle’s wheels drive electrical generation as it slows. The resulting electricity returns to the traction battery, where it can support later propulsion. Some vehicles use the same motor-generator for both driving and energy recovery, reversing the direction of useful energy flow.

evidence.locator: Key Components: Electric generator; traction motor
evidence.note: Wheel-driven generation, battery return and dual motor-generator role.

relations.note: Regeneration uses an electric-drive vehicle’s traction motor/generator and battery to turn wheel motion into energy available for later propulsion.

concepts.label: Graph theory
concepts.learning_takeaway: Represent real connections with vertices and edges, preserving adjacency rather than physical geography.
concepts.card: Graph theory models objects as vertices and connections as edges. In the Königsberg bridges problem, land areas become vertices and bridges become edges. The model keeps the crossing relationships while discarding the map’s detailed shapes, turning a walking puzzle into a question about traversing edges.
concepts.original_description: Studying networks of vertices and connecting edges.

evidence.locator: Königsberg bridge abstraction and vertex/edge definitions
evidence.note: Mapping land and bridges to graph elements; ignoring irrelevant geography.

relations.note: The bridge abstraction leads to the explicit question whether every edge can be traversed once, exactly the Euler-trail problem.

imported_records.description: Studying networks of vertices and connecting edges.

concepts.label: Java (programming language)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish compiled bytecode from source text and the virtual machine that executes it.
concepts.card: Java is a programming language whose source code can be compiled into bytecode and executed by a Java virtual machine. The development tools separate writing, compilation, and execution, although source-file launching can combine the last two steps for a small program.
concepts.original_description: An object-oriented programming language.

evidence.locator: The Compilation and Execution Cycle in Java; troubleshooting Java VM
evidence.note: Bytecode workflow, virtual-machine execution and source-file launching.

relations.note: The Java workflow explicitly uses a compiler to translate source text into bytecode before virtual-machine execution.

imported_records.description: An object-oriented programming language.

concepts.label: Python list comprehensions
concepts.learning_takeaway: Combine transformation, iteration and optional filtering into a new list, contrasted with resumable generation.
concepts.card: A Python list comprehension builds a new list by applying an expression across one or more iteration clauses, optionally filtering with conditions. The clauses keep their loop-like order, so changing which loop comes first can change the resulting order of combinations.

evidence.note: New-list construction, optional filters and preservation of clause ordering.

relations.note: A comprehension is a Python construct that expresses a list-producing loop and optional selection in one expression.
Editorial iteration comparison: list comprehensions produce a completed list, whereas generator functions preserve execution state between requested values.

concepts.label: Dendrochronology
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how annual growth rings preserve both time and environmental variation.
concepts.card: A tree’s rings record more than its age. Dendrochronology studies annual growth patterns to date wood and reconstruct environmental variation. Wide and narrow rings reflect changing growth conditions; matching a preserved sequence to calendar years can help date archaeological remains.

evidence.locator: Dendrochronology: The Study of Tree Rings; paragraphs on annual rings and crossdating
evidence.note: Annual rings, growth conditions, calendar matching and archaeological use.

relations.note: Calendar-dated tree rings provide chronological evidence for preserved wood at archaeological sites.

concepts.label: Tree-ring crossdating
concepts.learning_takeaway: Match overlapping ring-width patterns to place wood on a calendar chronology.
concepts.card: Tree-ring crossdating matches patterns of wide and narrow rings across different trees. Overlapping sequences from living trees and older preserved wood can extend a chronology beyond one tree’s lifetime, anchoring archaeological samples to calendar years rather than merely counting their rings.

evidence.locator: Dendrochronology: The Study of Tree Rings; paragraphs on annual rings and crossdating
evidence.note: Pattern matching among living and preserved trees extends chronologies.

relations.note: Crossdating is the ring-pattern matching procedure that links samples into a dendrochronological chronology.

concepts.label: Terminus post quem
concepts.learning_takeaway: Separate an earliest possible deposition date from an exact date.
concepts.card: A terminus post quem is an earliest possible date. For an undisturbed archaeological deposit, a coin minted in 1850 would rule out burial before 1850. It would not prove burial during that year: the object could have circulated before entering the ground.

evidence.note: TPQ lower-bound rule; hypothetical coin applies that rule.

relations.note: Archaeologists use the latest eligible artifact date to constrain when a deposit could first have formed.

concepts.label: Mean ceramic dating
concepts.learning_takeaway: Estimate occupation from a ceramic assemblage rather than dating a deposit by one object.
concepts.card: Mean ceramic dating uses a group of pottery fragments to estimate a site’s occupation period. Known production dates of ceramic types are combined across the assemblage. The resulting average concerns the collection’s chronology; it does not establish the exact burial date of every sherd.

evidence.locator: Ceramic assemblage and mean ceramic date paragraphs
evidence.note: Ceramic production dates and assemblage mean as occupation estimate.

relations.note: Historical archaeologists combine ceramic production chronologies to estimate the occupation represented by an assemblage.

concepts.label: Fire alteration of obsidian hydration evidence
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize that heating can invalidate a dating surface without requiring complete artifact destruction.
concepts.card: An obsidian tool can survive a fire while losing useful dating evidence. Heating may alter its surface enough to invalidate obsidian hydration dating. The problem separates two kinds of preservation: a recognizable artifact can remain even after the surface information needed for dating has changed.

evidence.locator: Wildfire impacts, paragraph beginning Wildland fires can impact archeological resources
evidence.note: Wildfire heat can alter a surface so hydration dating is unusable.

relations.note: Fire-related surface alteration is a documented limitation on using obsidian hydration to infer an artifact’s age.

concepts.label: Harris matrix
concepts.learning_takeaway: Represent relative stratigraphic relationships that one excavation profile cannot capture.
concepts.card: A Harris matrix diagrams the relative order of archaeological deposits and surfaces. A single section through a site cannot necessarily show all their relationships. Combining records into a matrix helps reconstruct how a complex site developed through time, beyond what physical depth alone can establish.

evidence.locator: The Harris Matrix and Its Significance to Archaeology; Changing the Stratigraphic Paradigm
evidence.note: Stratigraphic units, surfaces, relative sequence and limitations of sections.

relations.note: The matrix organizes excavated units and surfaces into a relative sequence for reconstructing an archaeological site’s development.

concepts.label: Archimedes Palimpsest
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how reuse of parchment preserved older mathematical texts underneath a prayer book.
concepts.card: The Archimedes Palimpsest is a medieval Greek prayer book made from reused parchment. Earlier writing was scraped away, and leaves were turned and folded again. Beneath the prayers survive mathematical texts, including Archimedes’ otherwise lost Method of Mechanical Theorems, showing how material reuse can preserve knowledge.

evidence.locator: The Book’s Contents; How Was it Made?
evidence.note: Reused parchment, rotated leaves, prayer text and surviving Method.

relations.note: Because this manuscript preserves an otherwise lost Archimedean treatise, it offers a material case for studying how historians recover ancient mathematics.

concepts.label: Minimal pair
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use a one-sound meaning contrast as evidence for separate phonemes.
concepts.card: Fan and van differ in just one speech sound and have different meanings in English. Such a minimal pair is evidence that the two sounds belong to different phonemes, or sound categories. The comparison concerns pronunciation, so matching or differing spellings alone cannot establish it.

evidence.locator: Video Script: fan/van and minimal-pair diagnosis
evidence.note: English fan/van, phonemic contrast and pronunciation rather than spelling.

relations.note: Comparing minimally different words is a phonological diagnostic for whether a sound difference distinguishes meaning.

concepts.label: Allophone
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish noncontrastive pronunciations of one phoneme from meaning-changing sound contrasts.
concepts.card: An allophone is one pronunciation variant within a phoneme, the sound category a language treats as a unit. English speakers can produce voiced and devoiced versions of l without changing a word’s identity. Many such variants are predictable from nearby sounds; others vary more freely.

evidence.locator: Opening definition; Video Script: noncontrastive variants and distribution
evidence.note: Noncontrastive l variants; conditioned distribution and free variation.

relations.note: Phonology investigates how a language organizes noncontrastive sound variants and their environments.
An allophone is a realization grouped within a phoneme; the distinction separates concrete variants from the sound category.

concepts.label: Allomorph
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize different forms that express one morpheme, including spoken plural variants.
concepts.card: The regular English plural has different spoken endings in cats, dogs, and buses, yet each adds the same plural meaning. These are allomorphs: alternative forms of one morpheme, a small meaning-bearing unit. Comparing them separates variation in pronunciation from a change in grammatical function.

evidence.locator: Opening definition; a/an and plural suffix examples
evidence.note: One plural morpheme has three spoken realizations with stable meaning.

relations.note: Allomorphs are alternative forms of meaning-bearing morphemes, making them units investigated in word-structure analysis.

concepts.label: Inflection (linguistics)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Separate grammatical changes to a word from creation of a new lexical word.
concepts.card: Inflection changes a word to express grammatical information such as number, tense, or case while retaining its core meaning and word class. Books adds plurality to book; sang marks past time for sing. Inflection can therefore involve an ending or a change inside the word.

evidence.locator: Opening definition; Video Script: number, tense, agreement and case
evidence.note: Grammatical information, retained category, plural endings and vowel-changing past forms.

relations.note: Inflection is the word-structure process that expresses grammatical distinctions such as number, tense and case.

concepts.label: Affixal derivation
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how affixes create new words, sometimes without changing grammatical category.
concepts.card: Affixal derivation creates a new word by adding a prefix or suffix to a base. Teach becomes teacher, changing a verb into a noun. Word class need not always change, and a derived base can take further affixes, as in computer, computerize, and computerization.

evidence.locator: Opening definition; Video Script: teach/teacher and category-preserving prefixes
evidence.note: Affix-based derivation, optional category change and repeated affixation.

evidence.locator: Video Script: contrast between affixation and compounding
evidence.note: Explicit boundary: affixation attaches bound morphemes, while compounding joins typically free morphemes.

relations.note: Affixal derivation is one way to create lexical words; compounding also forms words but joins typically free morphemes instead of attaching a bound affix.
The textbook contrasts creating a new word by derivation with supplying grammatical forms through inflection.

concepts.label: Constituency tests
concepts.learning_takeaway: Combine replacement and movement evidence to test which words act as a unit.
concepts.card: Words that act together as a sentence unit form a constituent. Linguists test candidate groups by replacing them, moving them, or using them as answers to questions. Agreement among tests supports an analysis, but a genuine constituent need not pass every test in every sentence.

evidence.locator: Replacement, Movement, Clefting, and Answers to Questions; final qualification
evidence.note: Replacement, movement, question answers and test limitations.

relations.note: These diagnostics apply linguistic observation to the specific problem of inferring which words group into phrases.

concepts.label: Free and bound morphemes
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish meaning-bearing units that stand alone from those requiring attachment.
concepts.card: A morpheme is a small unit pairing form with meaning. Some, such as cook, can stand alone; others, such as the past-tense -ed in cooked, must attach to another form. This free–bound distinction explains why meaningful pieces need not be independent words.

evidence.locator: Video Script: free and bound morphemes; cooked and carrots
evidence.note: Morpheme definition; free occurrence versus required attachment; cooked.

relations.note: Morphological analysis distinguishes units that can occur alone from units whose distribution requires attachment.

concepts.label: Structural ambiguity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Identify alternative phrase attachments that change meaning without changing word senses.
concepts.card: In “I saw the person with the telescope,” the telescope might belong to the person or be the instrument of seeing. Structural ambiguity comes from different ways of grouping the same words. It differs from ambiguity caused by a single word having several meanings.

evidence.locator: Structural ambiguity: Hilary/pirate/telescope example; lexical ambiguity contrast
evidence.note: Alternative prepositional-phrase attachments; structural versus lexical ambiguity.

relations.note: Alternative phrase attachments offer linguistic evidence that sentence structure contributes to meaning beyond individual word senses.
Constituency diagnostics help test the competing phrase groupings that produce a structurally ambiguous reading.

concepts.label: Focalization
concepts.learning_takeaway: Separate restrictions on narrative information from the identity of the speaker.
concepts.card: In Gérard Genette’s framework, focalization concerns which information a narrative makes available. A story may restrict itself to one character’s knowledge even when someone else narrates. Separating access to information from the identity of the speaker makes narrative viewpoint more precise than a first-person/third-person label.

evidence.locator: Definition; Explication, paragraphs on knowledge restrictions and voice
evidence.note: Information restriction; distinction between focalization and narrator/voice.

relations.note: Focalization gives literary criticism a way to analyze information limits separately from the narrator’s identity.

concepts.label: Free indirect discourse
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize the blend of narratorial grammar and a character’s expressions or viewpoint.
concepts.card: Free indirect discourse can retain a narrator’s third-person pronouns and past tense while borrowing a character’s expressions, judgments, or sense of “now.” The result blends voices without a clear “she thought” frame. Context often matters more than a single grammatical marker for recognizing the technique.

evidence.note: Mixed person/tense and expressive cues; absence of frame; contextual recognition.

relations.note: The technique offers literary critics a specific way to track interaction between narratorial wording and a character’s thought or speech.

concepts.label: Narrative metalepsis
concepts.learning_takeaway: Notice crossings between the level of telling and the world being told.
concepts.card: Narrative metalepsis crosses the boundary between telling a story and inhabiting it. A narrator might enter the action, or a fictional character might intrude into the narrator’s world. Such crossings can produce comic or fantastic effects by disturbing levels that the narrative normally keeps separate.

evidence.note: Crossing narrative levels; narrator/character intrusion; comic or fantastic effects.

relations.note: Metalepsis identifies a particular level-crossing device that literary criticism can distinguish from ordinary narration inside one story world.

concepts.label: Unreliable narration
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish factual reporting from interpretation and evaluation when assessing a narrator.
concepts.card: An unreliable narrator need not lie about what happened. A narrator may report events accurately yet misunderstand them or judge them in ways the text undermines. Critics therefore distinguish reporting, interpreting, and evaluating, using clues such as contradictions within the account or clashes with other characters.

evidence.locator: Definition; Explication; Features and Causes of Unreliability
evidence.note: Three narratorial functions; accurate reporting with unreliable interpretation; textual clues.

relations.note: This distinction structures critical reading of gaps between a narrator’s account and the implications of the surrounding text.

concepts.label: Analepsis
concepts.learning_takeaway: Track a return to earlier events relative to a story’s current narrative position.
concepts.card: Analepsis takes a narrative back to events earlier than its current position. In the Aeneid, books two and three recount happenings that precede book one. Separating the order of telling from the order of events shows how a flashback rearranges a story without changing its chronology.

evidence.note: Flashback definition and Aeneid books 2–3 example.

relations.note: Tracking analepsis is a specific method for analyzing how literary narration reorganizes event order.

concepts.label: Prolepsis (narrative)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Identify an anticipation of later events that interrupts chronological narrative order.
concepts.card: A narrative can disclose later events before reaching them. This is prolepsis, or a flashforward. In the Aeneid’s sixth book, the vision of Augustus anticipates a future beyond Aeneas’ own story, linking a character’s present to the later world familiar to the poem’s audience.

evidence.note: Flashforward definition; Aeneid book 6 and Augustus anticipation.

relations.note: Prolepsis names a forward shift that critics use to distinguish narrated order from chronological event order.
The source contrasts forward anticipation with retrospective narration as opposite disruptions of chronological order.

concepts.label: Ekphrasis
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how writing can interpret or animate visual art instead of merely describing it.
concepts.card: Ekphrasis uses language to describe or respond to visual art. A poem can do more than list what a painting contains: it may question the image, imagine a figure speaking, or reflect on viewing it. The artwork becomes a starting point for interpretation as well as description.

evidence.note: Visual-art response; interpretation, imagined speech and reflection beyond description.

relations.note: Editorial classification: this verbal literary response to visual art belongs within literature; the cited poetic examples show one form rather than an exhaustive parent field.

concepts.label: Engraving (printmaking)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how burin-cut lines and their thickness build printed tone.
concepts.card: In engraving, a burin cuts sharp grooves directly into a metal plate. The printmaker varies line thickness, spacing, and crossing strokes to suggest texture and shadow. A shaded form can therefore emerge from carefully organized lines rather than from a continuous painted wash.

evidence.locator: Main text: burin; Schongauer’s strokes; Cort’s swelling lines
evidence.note: Burin-cut grooves; varied strokes, crosshatching and line thickness.

relations.note: Engraving is a printmaking method that builds the image through grooves mechanically cut into a metal matrix.

concepts.label: Etching (printmaking)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Follow how acid converts lines drawn through a protective ground into printable grooves.
concepts.card: Etching lets acid do the cutting. An artist scratches a design through an acid-resistant coating on a metal plate; acid then bites the exposed lines. Longer exposure deepens them. After the coating is removed, those incisions provide the image for an intaglio print.

evidence.note: Ground, needle exposure, acid biting, depth and intaglio printing.

relations.note: Etching produces an intaglio printing matrix by chemically biting exposed areas of a coated metal plate.
Both form metal-plate incisions, but the source contrasts etching’s acid action with engraving’s direct burin cutting.

concepts.label: Aquatint
concepts.learning_takeaway: Create tonal areas through a granular acid-resistant ground instead of relying on drawn outlines.
concepts.card: Aquatint creates areas of printed tone using a grain of acid-resistant material on a metal plate. Acid bites between the protected particles, producing a textured surface. Different depths yield different tonal effects, while ordinary line etching often supplies outlines that the tonal process does not provide.

evidence.note: Granular resist, acid-biting depth, tone and combination with line etching.

relations.note: Aquatint adapts acid biting to a granular ground so an etched plate holds tonal areas rather than just linear marks.

concepts.label: Drypoint
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect a scratched plate’s fragile burr with its characteristic velvety printed lines.
concepts.card: A drypoint needle scratches directly into a metal plate, pushing up a ridge called a burr beside each line. That ridge holds extra ink and produces a rich, velvety mark. Because the burr wears during printing, later impressions can lose the effect that makes early ones distinctive.

evidence.note: Scratched line, ink-holding burr, velvety effect and wear.

relations.note: Drypoint is an intaglio process in which scratched metal and its retained burr carry the ink.

concepts.label: Mezzotint
concepts.learning_takeaway: Build light areas by smoothing an initially ink-holding roughened plate.
concepts.card: Mezzotint begins with a roughened metal plate that would print dark all over. The artist scrapes and burnishes selected areas so they retain less ink and appear lighter. Instead of building shadows mainly from lines, the image develops through controlled transitions from dark to light.

evidence.note: Roughened dark ground; scraping and burnishing create lighter tones.

relations.note: Mezzotint makes an intaglio image by selectively smoothing an initially rough, ink-holding metal surface.

concepts.label: Lithography (printmaking)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Separate a flat ink-selective printing surface from cut relief or incised processes.
concepts.card: Lithography prints from a flat surface rather than carved relief or grooves. A greasy drawing on prepared stone or metal attracts ink, while damp non-image areas repel it. The resulting separation lets a drawing’s marks transfer to paper without making its outlines into physical cuts.

evidence.note: Flat prepared matrix; greasy ink-receptive areas and damp ink-repellent areas.

relations.note: Lithography transfers an image using chemically differentiated areas of a flat printing matrix.

concepts.label: Multicolor screenprint registration
concepts.learning_takeaway: Keep successive color stencils aligned with one sheet during repeated printing.
concepts.card: A multicolor screenprint may use a different stencil for each color. Registration keeps each pass aligned with the same sheet, so separate printed shapes meet as intended. The task concerns the relationship among screen, paper, and successive impressions, beyond making any one stencil correctly.

evidence.locator: Preparing and Printing a Screen; multicolor registration paragraph
evidence.note: Different stencils per color and registration of paper and screen.

relations.note: Registration is the multicolor screenprinting task of maintaining alignment between successive stencils and the receiving sheet.

concepts.label: Woodcut
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize why uncut raised wood prints the image and can share a press with type.
concepts.card: A woodcut is made by removing wood around the lines and shapes meant to print. Ink sits on the surviving raised surface. Because movable type also prints in relief, woodblocks could be placed beside type and printed together, helping integrate illustrations with text in early books.

evidence.note: Relief image, removal of nonprinting wood, and printing alongside type.

relations.note: Woodcut is a relief process in which the raised parts of a carved woodblock transfer ink to paper.

concepts.label: Langar
concepts.learning_takeaway: Relate common food and equal seating to Sikh commitments to human equality.
concepts.card: Langar is the communal meal offered to everyone at a Sikh gurdwara. Sharing food and sitting at the same level express human equality across social divisions. The meal is vegetarian to make sharing easier across religious lines; that does not mean all Sikhs are themselves vegetarian.

evidence.locator: Summary; communal equality and vegetarian meal paragraphs
evidence.note: Open communal meal, equal seating, equality, and reason for vegetarian food.

relations.note: Langar puts Sikh commitments to equality and hospitality into practice through a shared meal open to visitors.

concepts.label: Cairo Genizah
concepts.learning_takeaway: Learn how a synagogue repository became evidence for ordinary life as well as sacred learning.
concepts.card: The Cairo Genizah preserved far more than worn sacred texts. The repository in Old Cairo’s Ben-Ezra Synagogue accumulated letters, accounts, and other documents over centuries. These fragments let historians study everyday Jewish life alongside religious learning, showing how a preservation custom can leave an unusually varied archive.

evidence.locator: Cairo’s dark chamber that remains a monument to life: repository practice paragraphs
evidence.note: Ben-Ezra repository and accumulation beyond worn sacred writing.

evidence.locator: Homepage description of Cairo Geniza and document genres
evidence.note: Letters, accounts and legal documents support everyday-life research.

relations.note: The collection preserves writings generated by Jewish religious practice together with evidence of the communities’ everyday lives.
The letters and accounts provide a concrete case of reconstructing historical experience from surviving primary material.

concepts.label: Eruv (carrying enclosure)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how a valid enclosure and shared food permit carrying within a joined Shabbat domain.
concepts.card: An eruv is a Jewish legal arrangement that permits carrying within a joined domain on Shabbat. It combines a valid enclosure with shared food that unites the residents. The boundaries follow religious-law requirements rather than property ownership, making activities such as taking a stroller outside possible.

evidence.locator: Definition; valid enclosure; shared food; uses
evidence.note: Valid enclosure, shared food, domain rules and carrying/stroller example.

relations.note: The eruv operates within Jewish Shabbat carrying rules by joining enclosed spaces and their residents into one domain.

concepts.label: Mihrab
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a prayer-direction niche from the direction it indicates, and see its ornamental role.
concepts.card: A mihrab is a niche indicating the direction of Mecca in a mosque or religious school. It gives prayer an architectural focus and can also carry elaborate ornament. The Met’s fourteenth-century Iranian example combines a recessed niche with cut-tile mosaics and religious inscriptions.

evidence.note: Prayer-direction niche; fourteenth-century Iranian tilework and inscriptions.

relations.note: The niche organizes sacred space around prayer direction while its ornament makes that directional focus visually prominent.

concepts.label: Shikinen Sengu at Ise
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand continuity maintained through periodic rebuilding and transfer rather than unchanged fabric.
concepts.card: At Ise Jingu, Shikinen Sengu follows a twenty-year renewal cycle. A new sanctuary is built on an adjacent alternate site, and sacred furnishings are remade before the divine symbol is transferred. Continuity here depends on repeating forms and rituals while replacing the buildings’ material fabric.

evidence.note: Twenty-year cycle, alternate site, renewed furnishings and transfer ritual.

relations.note: Ise’s renewal culminates in transferring the sacred symbol within a continuing Shinto ritual cycle.
The rebuilding practice offers a specific comparison between continuity of sacred architectural form and preservation of original building fabric.

concepts.label: Tawaf
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish circling the Kaaba from the separate passage between Safa and Marwah.
concepts.card: Tawaf is the ritual of circling the Kaaba seven times counterclockwise. In Hajj, the shared movement expresses devotion and communal unity. It differs from Sa’i, the separate passage between Safa and Marwah, so similar-looking crowds may be performing distinct acts within the larger pilgrimage.

evidence.locator: Circumambulation of the Kaaba; Safa and Marwah
evidence.note: Seven counterclockwise circuits; symbolic meaning; distinction from Sa’i.

relations.note: Tawaf is a specified circling ritual in the Hajj sequence, distinct from its other movements and stations.

concepts.label: Geoid
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand the idealized gravity-shaped sea surface used as a reference for elevation.
concepts.card: The geoid models the sea surface after removing tides and currents, extended mathematically through the continents. Its gentle irregularities reflect Earth’s uneven gravitational field. Surveyors use this reference surface when determining elevations, so “height above sea level” involves a physical model rather than a perfectly smooth globe.

evidence.locator: Main explanation of idealized sea surface and elevations
evidence.note: Idealized sea surface, gravity variations, continental extension and elevations.

relations.note: Geodesy uses gravity observations and the geoid model to supply a physical reference for measuring elevations.

concepts.label: Rhumb line
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why a straight Mercator-chart line is convenient for maintaining a constant course.
concepts.card: A rhumb line keeps a constant course. On a Mercator chart it appears straight, so a navigator can measure its angle against the meridians to determine a steering direction. This links a projection’s geometry to the practical task of following a course at sea.

evidence.locator: Map Projections: Mercator and rhumb lines
evidence.note: Constant course, straight Mercator representation and meridian-angle measurement.

relations.note: A constant-course line becomes a practical navigation tool because Mercator charts allow its steering direction to be measured directly.

concepts.label: Universal Transverse Mercator grid
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize zone-based planar coordinates as an alternative position notation, not inherently greater accuracy.
concepts.card: The Universal Transverse Mercator system locates points within sixty zones, normally six degrees of longitude wide. Its plane-coordinate grids offer an alternative to latitude and longitude. Choosing UTM can make certain maps easier to use, but the notation is not inherently more accurate than geographic coordinates.

evidence.note: Sixty-zone plane grid and no inherent accuracy advantage over latitude/longitude.

relations.note: UTM supplies a zone-based plane coordinate framework that cartographers can place on maps to identify locations.

concepts.label: Tissot’s indicatrix
concepts.learning_takeaway: Read projected ellipses as local evidence of angle and area distortion.
concepts.card: Tissot’s indicatrix makes local map distortion visible with projected circles and ellipses. On a conformal map the markers stay circular but can change size; on an equal-area map their areas remain equal while shapes change. Repeating the markers shows how distortion varies from place to place.

evidence.locator: Opening explanation; conformal and equal-area comparisons
evidence.note: Local ellipses; conformal circles; equal-area markers; spatial variation.

relations.note: Indicatrices visualize the local scale, angular and areal distortions introduced by a map projection.

concepts.label: Cartographic generalization
concepts.learning_takeaway: Reduce map detail while preserving important spatial relationships between features.
concepts.card: Making a smaller-scale map requires deciding what to omit, simplify, or emphasize. Cartographic generalization must also preserve relationships: smoothing a river could detach it from a bridge or move it through a building. Clear maps therefore require contextual decisions, not just fewer points and thinner detail.

evidence.locator: What is generalization?; river/bridge example; workflow
evidence.note: Selection/simplification and contextual river, bridge and building conflicts.

relations.note: Generalization is the cartographic process of reducing complexity for scale while preserving recognizable landscape patterns and relationships.

concepts.label: Magnetic declination
concepts.learning_takeaway: Account for the changing angle between local magnetic north and true north.
concepts.card: A compass follows the local magnetic field, which need not align with true north. The angle between those directions is magnetic declination. Because it changes with both location and time, converting a compass direction to true north requires a correction appropriate to where and when you measure.

evidence.locator: Magnetic Declination; FAQ on compass direction
evidence.note: Local field direction; angle from true north; location/time dependence.

relations.note: Declination is the directional correction needed when navigation combines magnetic-compass observations with true-north bearings.

concepts.label: History
concepts.learning_takeaway: Treat accounts of the past as evidence-based interpretations that can change.
concepts.card: History investigates the human past through surviving objects, writing, and oral traditions. These traces require interpretation: accounts can change when evidence is questioned or new perspectives are considered. A diary, an artifact, and a later historian’s argument can therefore answer different questions about the same past.
concepts.original_description: past events and their documentation, studied through historiography, archaeology, and related disciplines

evidence.locator: Discipline Profile and Core Concepts; Develop historical methods
evidence.note: Artifacts, writing, oral traditions, interpretation and revisable knowledge.

relations.note: Historical interpretation can draw on archaeology’s material sequences alongside written and oral evidence.
Oral history supplies recorded recollections that historians interpret in context alongside other surviving evidence.

imported_records.description: past events and their documentation, studied through historiography, archaeology, and related disciplines

concepts.label: Linguistics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish observing language patterns from prescribing preferred usage.
concepts.card: Linguistics studies how human language works by observing patterns in what people actually say. It asks why some sounds or structures occur and others do not. Comparing fan with van, for example, turns an ordinary pronunciation difference into evidence about the sound categories English speakers use.
concepts.original_description: Studying the structures, meanings and uses of human language.

evidence.locator: Video Script: empirical observation and descriptive approach
evidence.note: Empirical observation and explanatory study of language use.

evidence.locator: Video Script: fan/van and minimal-pair diagnosis
evidence.note: Fan/van is evidence for contrasting English sound categories.

relations.note: Phonology is a concrete direction within linguistic inquiry: it investigates which sound differences a language uses to distinguish meaning.
Morphology extends the investigation from speech sounds to how small meaning-bearing units form words.

imported_records.description: Studying the structures, meanings and uses of human language.

concepts.label: Java (island)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize the Indonesian island’s volcanic spine without confusing its name with a programming language.
concepts.card: Java, the Indonesian island, has an east–west chain of volcanic mountains running through its interior. It is also home to several major languages, including Javanese and Sundanese. Studying the island therefore involves both a distinctive physical landscape and linguistic differences within one geographic place.
concepts.original_description: An island of Indonesia.

evidence.locator: Disambiguation note; lead paragraphs on volcanic spine and languages
evidence.note: Island identity, volcanic spine and major languages.

relations.note: Java’s volcanic mountain chain offers a specific case for studying how physical landforms organize an island’s landscape.
The presence of Javanese, Sundanese and other languages makes Java a geographic case for examining multilingual societies.

imported_records.description: An island of Indonesia.

concepts.label: Rosetta Stone
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish three scripts from two languages and parallel texts from exact translations.
concepts.card: The Rosetta Stone presents related versions of a decree in three scripts but two languages: Egyptian in hieroglyphic and Demotic writing, and Greek. The comparison helped decipher Egyptian scripts, yet the versions do not match word for word. A multilingual key still requires interpretation.
concepts.original_description: ancient Egyptian stele with inscriptions in three writing systems

evidence.locator: Lead; Later work: versions cannot be matched word for word
evidence.note: Two languages, three scripts, decipherment and non-identical versions.

relations.note: The parallel inscriptions make script, language and meaning separable questions, a concrete bridge to linguistic analysis rather than simple visual symbol matching.

imported_records.description: ancient Egyptian stele with inscriptions in three writing systems
imported_records.subsection: Language and Literature / Language / Alphabets and writing systems

concepts.label: The Tale of Genji
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect a courtly narrative to its reinterpretation in varied visual media.
concepts.card: Written in early-eleventh-century Japan, Murasaki Shikibu’s Tale of Genji follows courtly relationships around the “Shining Prince.” Its later artistic life extends through paintings, calligraphy, silk robes, and manga. The same literary scenes can be approached through different materials and visual conventions as well as through prose.

evidence.note: Author, early-eleventh-century court narrative and visual-art adaptations.

relations.note: The museum describes Genji as a psychological novel centered on courtly relationships.
Genji-inspired visual art moves from words to images; ekphrastic writing moves from images to words. Comparing the directions can clarify how media transform a subject.

concepts.label: Under the Wave off Kanagawa
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how Hokusai’s composition makes Mount Fuji look small inside a looming wave.
concepts.card: Hokusai’s Under the Wave off Kanagawa places Mount Fuji inside the hollow of a towering wave, making the mountain look unexpectedly small. Part of Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, this woodblock design uses perspective to make scale and visual importance diverge within one dramatic composition.

evidence.note: Hokusai, series, medium and perspective making Fuji appear small.
Woodcut process supports the broader printmaking relation.

relations.note: The museum identifies the work as a woodblock print; the woodcut process explains how raised carved surfaces can produce impressions of such a design.

concepts.label: Language revitalization
concepts.learning_takeaway: See how everyday immersion creates opportunities to use and transmit a community’s language.
concepts.card: Language revitalization can happen through ordinary activities as well as formal lessons. In British Columbia’s Mentor-Apprentice Program, learners spend one-to-one immersion time with fluent speakers, bringing a First Nations language into home life and activities on land and water. Continued use becomes part of daily routines.
concepts.original_description: Supporting the continued use and transmission of threatened languages.

evidence.note: One-on-one immersion and language use at home, on land and on water.

relations.note: The mentor-apprentice example applies language learning to rebuilding regular use of a community’s language through everyday immersion.

imported_records.description: Supporting the continued use and transmission of threatened languages.

concepts.label: Silk Road
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how a trading network also supported movement of religious communities.
concepts.card: The Silk Road names a network of routes, not one continuous highway. Its connections carried beliefs as well as goods. Buddhist monasteries offered lodging to traveling merchants, while merchants supported monasteries, illustrating a practical relationship between trade infrastructure and the movement of religious communities.
concepts.original_description: trade routes through Asia connecting China to the Mediterranean Sea

evidence.locator: Name and contested significance; Transmission of Buddhism, merchants/monasteries paragraphs
evidence.note: Network of routes; merchant support and monastery accommodation.

relations.note: Merchant support of monasteries and monastery lodging for travelers connected trade routes with Buddhism’s movement across regions.

imported_records.description: trade routes through Asia connecting China to the Mediterranean Sea
imported_records.subsection: History / Prehistory and Ancient history / Asia

concepts.label: Information asymmetry
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish unequal information between trading parties from uncertainty shared by both.
concepts.card: Information asymmetry occurs when one side of a transaction knows more than the other. A used-car seller may know defects that a buyer cannot see. This differs from uncertainty that both parties share, and helps explain why inspections, warranties, and reputations matter.

evidence.locator: Opening definitions; Mechanisms to Reduce the Risk of Imperfect Information
evidence.note: Defines unequal information; used-car and warranty/reputation examples explain possible responses.

relations.note: Unequal knowledge changes participation and quality assessment in exchange; this is a specific economic mechanism within the broader study of markets.

concepts.label: Moral hazard
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how protection from consequences can change behavior after an agreement.
concepts.card: Moral hazard arises when protection from a loss changes incentives to avoid it. An insured business might invest less in theft prevention because an insurer bears part of the cost. Deductibles leave some losses with the policyholder, potentially preserving incentives for care.

evidence.note: Business security example and deductibles show changed incentives under coverage.

relations.note: The shift in incentives when another party bears costs is an economic problem of behavior under a contract; insurance supplies the documented example.

concepts.label: Adverse selection
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace how privately known risk changes who chooses to buy coverage.
concepts.card: Adverse selection can occur when buyers privately know their risk better than insurers. A premium based on average risk may discourage safer buyers, leaving a costlier pool. Further price increases can worsen that sorting, even without anyone changing their behavior after buying coverage.

evidence.note: Private risk information and the departing low-risk buyers example support the selection spiral.

relations.note: Privately known characteristics alter which exchanges occur; this economic sorting mechanism differs from changes in behavior once a contract exists.

concepts.label: Actuarially fair insurance
concepts.learning_takeaway: Separate an expected-claims premium from one that also covers expenses and profit.
concepts.card: An actuarially fair insurance premium equals expected claims for the relevant risk group. It is a pricing benchmark, not a judgment about social fairness. A real insurer also needs to cover operating expenses and, where applicable, profit, so an actual premium can exceed expected payouts.

evidence.locator: Risk Groups and Actuarial Fairness; How Insurance Works
evidence.note: Expected-loss benchmark and the stated claims/expenses/profit accounting support the distinction.

relations.note: The source defines actuarial fairness as a benchmark for insurance premiums using expected claims in a risk group.

concepts.label: Signaling in economics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how observable credentials convey information about less observable attributes.
concepts.card: Signaling in economics uses something observable to convey information about something harder to inspect. Employers may treat educational credentials or awards as clues to an applicant’s abilities and persistence. The signal helps shape judgment under uncertainty; possessing the credential is not identical to demonstrating every relevant skill.

evidence.locator: Labor-market example, paragraphs on credentials, awards, and references
evidence.note: The employer example identifies credentials and accolades as signals of difficult-to-observe attributes.

relations.note: Observable credentials are used in market decisions when productivity is hard to observe; that information mechanism belongs within economics.

concepts.label: The Market for Lemons
aliases: The Market for Lemons: Quality Uncertainty and the Market Mechanism
concepts.learning_takeaway: Read Akerlof’s used-car model as a mechanism by which hidden quality can drive good products out of trade.
concepts.card: George Akerlof’s 1970 paper The Market for Lemons uses used cars to model hidden quality. If buyers cannot distinguish good cars from bad ones, the price they offer can discourage owners of good cars from selling, worsening the quality available for trade.

evidence.locator: Original pp.488–489, Introduction and II.A; PDF pp.2–3
evidence.note: Title, authorship, year, illustrative automobile market, asymmetric knowledge, and withdrawal of good cars are established on the inspected pages.

relations.note: Akerlof explicitly models sellers knowing car quality better than buyers and shows how this asymmetric information affects which cars trade.

concepts.label: Fivefold repetition in chess
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish an automatic repetition draw from a player’s threefold-repetition claim.
concepts.card: Under FIDE’s 2023 laws, five appearances of the same chess position end the game in a draw without a player’s claim. Identical piece placement alone is insufficient: the player to move and available moves must also match, including relevant castling and en passant rights.

evidence.note: Defines position identity and the automatic five-occurrence draw; commentary explicitly requires arbiter intervention.

relations.note: The drawn-game articles specify this chess termination condition and define which positions count as repetitions.

concepts.label: Seventy-five-move rule
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand an automatic draw after 75 moves by each player without pawn moves or captures, with checkmate taking precedence.
concepts.card: FIDE’s 2023 seventy-five-move rule automatically draws a chess game after 75 moves by each player without a pawn move or capture. Counting both players’ moves matters. If the final move delivers checkmate, however, that result takes precedence over this automatic draw.

evidence.note: The rule gives the per-player count, both resetting events, automatic intervention, and checkmate exception.

relations.note: This rule limits a chess game’s continuation using a counter reset by pawn moves or captures, with an explicit checkmate exception.

concepts.label: Castling in Chess960
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain how varied starting squares still lead to standard king and rook castling destinations.
concepts.card: Chess960 varies the starting arrangement, but castling finishes with the king and rook on the usual castling squares. On the g-side, the king ends on g1 or g8 and the rook on f1 or f8. Depending on their starting squares, one piece may remain stationary.

evidence.locator: Guidelines II.1 and II.3; PDF pp.57–58
evidence.note: Randomized setup, invariant castling destinations, and king-only or rook-only movement are explicit.

relations.note: Chess960 preserves ordinary piece movement and checkmate while adapting castling to randomized back ranks; this is a specific variant-rule connection to chess.

concepts.label: Finesse in bridge
concepts.learning_takeaway: Use play order to try to win with an intermediate honor when an opponent holds a higher card.
concepts.card: A finesse in bridge tries to win a trick with a card below an opponent’s highest card in that suit. Leading toward an ace–queen holding can let the queen win when the missing king lies with the opponent who must play before that holding.

evidence.note: The low lead toward ace–queen succeeds against the king held by the intervening opponent.

relations.note: ACBL teaches this leading technique as part of declarer’s play of a bridge hand, specifically to win an additional trick.

concepts.label: Pie rule
concepts.learning_takeaway: Show why letting the second player swap sides changes the incentive behind the opening move.
concepts.card: The pie rule lets the second player choose sides after seeing the opening move. In Hex, an overwhelmingly strong first placement may simply be taken over by the opponent. This gives the first player a reason to choose a more balanced opening instead.

evidence.note: The ordinary Hex swap procedure and its effect on opening incentives are explicit.

relations.note: Swapping ownership after the opening placement changes incentives in alternating board games; Hex provides the inspected implementation.

concepts.label: Projex
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect winning loops in a projective-plane game to the topology of its board.
concepts.card: Projex is a connection game played on a representation of the real projective plane. Players color tiles to form a loop that cannot shrink to a point on that surface. Its spherical display pairs opposite tiles, making an abstract topological identification part of every move.

evidence.note: Defines Projective Hex, noncontractible winning cycles, the antipodal sphere representation, and paired coloring.

relations.note: Players alternately occupy a defined board to meet a connection objective; this makes the named topological game a concrete board-game example.

concepts.label: Encoding specificity principle
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why a cue works through overlap with how an event was encoded.
concepts.card: A memory cue works partly by matching information encoded with the original experience. A song can bring back a particular conversation because both were linked at the time. Encoding specificity explains why the effectiveness of a reminder depends on how the event was originally remembered.

evidence.note: The song/party/conversation example and overlap-with-encoding principle support the explanation.

relations.note: The memory chapter states this principle as an account of which retrieval cues evoke a stored experience.

Both concern encoding–retrieval compatibility. The navigation comparison separates cue–trace information overlap from matching the cognitive operations performed during study and test; it does not claim the theories are wholly independent.

concepts.label: Cue overload principle
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why a cue linked to many memories is less diagnostic of the desired one.
concepts.card: A reminder loses precision when it points to too many memories. “Recall the picture” identifies a lone picture among words more effectively than one picture among many. The cue overload principle adds an important condition to retrieval: a cue should distinguish the desired memory from competitors.

evidence.note: Contrasts a single picture with multiple pictures and explains the need for a distinctive cue–target relationship.

relations.note: Cue overload is presented as a principle governing retrieval from memory when one cue matches multiple traces.

concepts.label: Recognition failure of recallable words
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish failing to recognize a word from lacking a retrievable memory of it.
concepts.card: Failing to recognize a word does not always mean it cannot be recalled. Someone may overlook Shaw in a list of authors yet supply it after “George Bernard.” Recognition failure of recallable words shows that the form of a retrieval cue can change apparent memory success.

evidence.note: The Shaw/George Bernard dissociation and its name are explicitly described.

relations.note: The source identifies an experimental dissociation between recognition and cued recall, both methods for measuring memory retrieval.

concepts.label: Retrieval-induced forgetting
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how practicing retrieval of selected items can impair recall of related unpracticed items.
concepts.card: Retrieving some memories can make related, unpracticed memories harder to recall. In Anderson and colleagues’ word-category experiments, participants practiced selected items, then recalled fewer unpracticed members of those categories on a later test. Measuring only practiced items can therefore miss other effects of the exercise.

evidence.note: The category practice design and delayed impairment of unpracticed related items establish the phenomenon.

relations.note: The experiment concerns long-term memory retrieval and selective later forgetting of related representations.

concepts.label: Attentional blink
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a temporary second-target reporting deficit from literal blinking.
concepts.card: The attentional blink is a brief difficulty detecting a second target after identifying a first one in a rapid visual stream. In the original letter experiment, detection fell during a window beginning 180 milliseconds after the target. Ignoring the first target removed that pattern.

evidence.note: Reports the rapid serial letter task, onset of the impaired interval, and absence when first-target identification is not required.

relations.note: The paper manipulates allocation of visual attention between rapidly presented targets and measures the resulting detection deficit.

concepts.label: Implementation intentions
concepts.learning_takeaway: Turn a goal into a cue-linked action plan with a specified if–then contingency.
concepts.card: Implementation intentions connect a specific cue to a planned response: if a chosen situation occurs, then a particular action follows. Unlike merely wanting an outcome, this plan spells out when and how to begin. Its usefulness depends partly on choosing a workable cue and an effective response.

evidence.locator: Overview; pp.6–7; Precision and Selecting an Effective Response, pp.9–12
evidence.note: If–then structure, goal/implementation distinction, specificity, viability, and instrumentality support the card.

relations.note: Cue-linked plans apply psychological mechanisms of attention and action regulation to carrying out goals; psychology is the broader field for this behavior-change method.

concepts.label: Cadential six-four chord
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a chord’s tonic pitch content from its dominant function at a cadence.
concepts.card: The cadential six-four uses the notes of a tonic triad with its fifth in the bass, yet commonly functions as part of the dominant at a cadence. Its usual move to the dominant chord shows why pitch content and harmonic function need not tell the same story.

evidence.note: Identifies I6/4 before V, dominant function, and the equivalent I/fifth notation.

relations.note: This chord’s position and resolution explain a specific relationship between chord spelling and harmonic function, making harmony the broader subject.

concepts.label: Tonicization
concepts.learning_takeaway: Hear a secondary dominant make a non-tonic chord a temporary harmonic goal.
concepts.card: Tonicization makes a chord other than the home chord behave as a local tonal goal. A secondary dominant approaches that chord as its own dominant would. In C major, D7 can lead strongly to G, temporarily giving the G chord a special sense of arrival.

evidence.note: Defines treating a non-I chord as tonic and identifies D7 as V/V progressing to G in C major.

relations.note: Secondary-dominant motion changes the local function of a chord within a harmonic progression; harmony is the broader organizing subject.

concepts.label: Common-tone modulation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace a single shared pitch used as a hinge between chords belonging to different keys.
concepts.card: Common-tone modulation connects different keys through a shared pitch. In a Beethoven example, C-sharp links a C-sharp major chord to an A dominant seventh chord, helping bridge F-sharp minor and D major. One held or repeated note can preserve continuity while its harmonic setting changes.

evidence.note: Defines a single-note bridge and explicitly identifies the C-sharp connection and surrounding keys.

relations.note: Reinterpreting one shared pitch across chords provides a concrete harmonic method of moving between tonal centers.

concepts.label: Melodic inversion
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish reversing melodic interval direction from changing note order.
concepts.card: Melodic inversion reverses the direction of a tune’s intervals, turning upward motion downward and vice versa. A real inversion preserves exact interval qualities; a tonal inversion adjusts them to stay within a key. The distinction explains how a recognizable mirrored shape can retain different pitch details.

evidence.note: Defines inversion and distinguishes real interval-quality preservation from tonal adaptation to scale or key.

relations.note: The source explicitly presents inversion as one method of altering a melody while relating it to its original motive.

concepts.label: Rhythmic augmentation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize proportionally lengthened note values while the motive remains identifiable.
concepts.card: Rhythmic augmentation lengthens a musical idea’s note values, commonly doubling every duration. A motive written in quarter notes can return in half notes while preserving its relative rhythm. The technique expands the idea in time rather than adding extra notes to extend the phrase.

evidence.locator: §11.2.3, definition and Bach Invention No.1 example
evidence.note: Defines usual doubling of durations and illustrates augmentation of a contrapuntal motive.

relations.note: Proportional expansion of note durations is a particular transformation of rhythmic organization; the Bach example supplies a compositional use.

concepts.label: Music for 18 Musicians
concepts.learning_takeaway: Hear fixed instrumental pulse against breath-length vocal and wind phrases in Reich’s work.
concepts.card: Steve Reich’s Music for 18 Musicians layers two kinds of musical time. Pianos and mallet instruments maintain a regular pulse, while voices and winds shape passages around the length of a breath. The resulting swells move against a steady beat rather than replacing it.

evidence.locator: Words from the Composer, printed p.10 / PDF p.11
evidence.note: Reich explicitly contrasts continuous piano/mallet pulse and breath-duration pulsing of voices and winds.

relations.note: The work provides a concrete comparison of metrical pulse and breathing-shaped phrase duration, two interacting ways of organizing musical time.

concepts.label: Doctrine of double effect
concepts.learning_takeaway: Separate intending harm as a means from foreseeing it as a side effect while retaining proportionality constraints.
concepts.card: The doctrine of double effect distinguishes harm intended as a means from harm foreseen as a side effect. It argues that the latter may sometimes be permissible when the former is not. Proportionality and other conditions matter; merely calling harm unintended does not automatically justify it.

evidence.note: The doctrine’s intended-means/foreseen-side-effect distinction and cumulative conditions are explicit.

relations.note: The entry presents double effect as a principle for judging the moral permissibility of actions with good and harmful effects.

concepts.label: Moral luck
concepts.learning_takeaway: Examine tension between judging people only for what they control and judging different outcomes differently.
concepts.card: Moral luck asks how events outside someone’s control can affect moral judgment. Two equally careless drivers might both suffer brake failure, yet only one encounters a person in the road. Judging them differently creates tension with the principle that blame should track what an agent controls.

evidence.note: The source contrasts the control principle with differently assessed negligent drivers and outcomes.

relations.note: The dispute concerns moral praise and blame when outcomes and circumstances escape an agent’s control.

concepts.label: Nonidentity problem
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why identity-changing choices complicate claims that a particular future person was made worse off.
concepts.card: A choice can change which future people exist, rather than simply improving the lives of the same people. The nonidentity problem asks how such a choice can wrong someone whose life is worth living if the alternative would have meant that particular person never existed.

evidence.locator: Introduction, person-affecting intuition and worthwhile-life qualification
evidence.note: Identity-affecting choices, person-affecting harm, and the worth-having-life assumption are explicitly discussed.

relations.note: The entry identifies the puzzle as a problem of population ethics and obligations toward possible future people.

concepts.label: Epistemic closure
concepts.learning_takeaway: Examine whether competent deduction from retained knowledge yields knowledge of the conclusion.
concepts.card: Epistemic closure asks whether knowledge survives competent deduction. A qualified principle requires knowing the premise, correctly deriving a conclusion, and believing it while retaining the original knowledge. Philosophers disagree partly because accepting closure constrains how ordinary knowledge claims can be reconciled with skeptical possibilities.

evidence.locator: Introduction; §1 K and SPK; rejection by Dretske and Nozick
evidence.note: Qualified deduction/retained-knowledge conditions and the relationship to skepticism support the explanation.

relations.note: Closure is a proposed constraint on how knowledge extends through inference, a central epistemological question.

concepts.label: Experience machine
concepts.learning_takeaway: Test whether simulated desirable experience would provide everything that makes a life go well.
concepts.card: Robert Nozick’s experience machine imagines a device that supplies a lifetime of desired experiences without the corresponding real achievements. Would plugging in provide everything that makes life good? The thought experiment challenges experience-only accounts of well-being, but disagreement about our intuitions keeps the argument open.

evidence.note: The imagined device, real achievement contrast, and caution about treating the objection as decisive are explicit.

relations.note: The thought experiment tests what constitutes a good life and therefore connects to ethical evaluation of well-being.

concepts.label: A Theory of Justice
concepts.learning_takeaway: See why Rawls deprives hypothetical choosers of knowledge of social advantages when selecting principles.
concepts.card: John Rawls’s 1971 book A Theory of Justice develops justice as fairness. Its hypothetical choice of social principles removes knowledge of personal advantages behind a veil of ignorance. Without knowing their eventual position, the choosers cannot tailor institutions simply to favor their own class or talents.

evidence.locator: §1 Life and Work; §4.6 The Original Position
evidence.note: Identifies the 1971 book and explains the informational restrictions preventing arbitrary advantage in the original position.

relations.note: The book offers an account of just social institutions by using hypothetical agreement, a concrete project in political philosophy.

concepts.label: Sainte-Laguë method
concepts.learning_takeaway: Allocate seats by ranking party-vote totals divided by successive odd numbers.
concepts.card: The Sainte-Laguë method turns party votes into seats by dividing each eligible party’s total by successive odd numbers: 1, 3, 5, and onward. The highest resulting quotients receive seats. Each selected quotient contributes another seat, making the rounding procedure explicit rather than leaving fractional seats unresolved.

evidence.note: Odd divisors, ranking quotients, and counting each party’s selected quotients establish the allocation algorithm.

relations.note: A democracy using proportional representation needs a rule for converting vote shares to whole seats; this is one documented allocation method.

concepts.label: Overhang seats
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand the extra seats created when constituency victories exceed a party’s proportional entitlement.
concepts.card: An overhang arises when a party wins more constituency seats than its proportional vote share would normally provide. Under New Zealand’s 2023 allocation rules, it keeps those extra seats, enlarging Parliament. Other parties retain their allocations, so constituency results can alter the legislature’s final size.

evidence.note: Explains excess electorate wins, no additional list seats, increased size, and unchanged other-party allocations.

relations.note: Mixed constituency-and-list representation can generate a mismatch between local victories and proportional entitlement; overhang rules resolve that electoral design problem.

concepts.label: Constructive vote of no confidence
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand replacing a head of government by agreeing on a successor in the same parliamentary procedure.
concepts.card: A constructive vote of no confidence removes a head of government only by agreeing on a replacement. In Germany, the Bundestag must elect a successor rather than merely reject the chancellor. A majority against the incumbent therefore does not suffice without a majority for another candidate.

evidence.note: The Bundestag glossary requires agreement on a new government head and a majority-supported successor.

relations.note: The Bundestag describes this as a parliamentary control mechanism that replaces the chancellor through election of a successor.

concepts.label: Notice-and-comment rulemaking
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish public participation in covered US administrative rules from simply announcing the final rule.
concepts.card: For many U.S. federal regulations, notice-and-comment rulemaking requires an agency to publish a proposal and let interested people submit written views or evidence. The agency then considers relevant submissions and states the adopted rule’s basis and purpose. Statutory exceptions mean this sequence does not govern every rule.

evidence.note: Notice, written participation, consideration, basis-and-purpose statement, and explicit exceptions are in the statute.

relations.note: This procedure governs how U.S. administrative agencies make covered rules, a specific process within administrative law.

concepts.label: Stratified sortition for citizens’ assemblies
concepts.learning_takeaway: Combine random invitations with demographic balancing rather than treating volunteers as a representative sample.
concepts.card: Stratified sortition combines chance with demographic balancing when recruiting a citizens’ assembly. Ireland first invites randomly selected households, then selects among applicants so the group broadly reflects characteristics such as age, gender, and geography. Random invitations alone would not perform this second balancing step.

evidence.note: The current recruitment account separates random household invitation from stratified selection using demographic information.

relations.note: The official assembly FAQ identifies this two-stage procedure as its method of selecting citizen members.

concepts.label: Irish Citizens’ Assembly (2016–2018)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect expert evidence, facilitated discussion, and secret ballots in a particular national assembly.
concepts.card: Ireland’s 2016–2018 Citizens’ Assembly combined expert information, public submissions, and discussion among selected citizens. Its procedures encouraged roundtable questioning and used secret ballots when voting was required. This particular assembly shows how learning, deliberation, and a formal decision procedure can be organized together.

evidence.note: The dated body and its documented evidence, presentations, roundtable discussion, and secret voting procedures establish the case.

relations.note: This is the named Irish implementation of a citizens’ assembly, with specified learning, discussion, and voting procedures.

concepts.label: Role conflict
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish incompatible demands across different social roles from pressure within one role.
concepts.card: Role conflict occurs when expectations attached to different social roles clash. A person’s responsibilities as an employee may demand staying late while responsibilities as a parent require leaving. The problem comes from incompatible roles, even when either role alone would be manageable.

evidence.note: The employee/parent example distinguishes contradictory roles from demands within one role.

relations.note: The sociology chapter locates role conflict in the expected behavior associated with multiple social statuses.

concepts.label: Role strain
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize competing demands within a single role even without a clash between separate roles.
concepts.card: Role strain is pressure from the many demands within a single social role. Parenting, for example, can combine practical work, problem-solving, and moral guidance. This differs from role conflict, where obligations tied to separate roles pull against one another; one role alone can be demanding enough.

evidence.note: Defines too much required of a single role and contrasts contradictory roles, with parenting tasks as illustration.

relations.note: Role strain is presented as a sociological consequence of demands attached to one social role.

concepts.label: Looking-glass self
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand how imagined judgments by other people feed into self-understanding.
concepts.card: Charles Cooley’s looking-glass self describes how self-understanding develops through imagined reactions from other people. We picture how we appear, interpret others’ responses, and form judgments about ourselves. The “mirror” is our interpretation of their viewpoint, so it need not accurately reveal what they actually think.

evidence.note: Cooley’s theory explicitly uses imagined appearance, inferred reactions, and resulting self-understanding.

relations.note: The social-interaction account explains formation of a sense of self through perceived appraisals, within the sociology chapter’s presentation-of-self discussion.

concepts.label: Weak ties
concepts.learning_takeaway: Explain why casual acquaintances can supply information beyond one’s close circle.
concepts.card: Weak ties are casual connections rather than close relationships. Granovetter’s explanation emphasizes their reach: an acquaintance can connect someone to a social circle beyond their usual contacts, bringing different information or opportunities. Their value depends on that position in the network, not simply on having many acquaintances.

evidence.locator: Opening discussion and Granovetter interview quotation
evidence.note: Defines casual connections and explains access to networks outside one’s own circle.

relations.note: Granovetter explicitly explains weak ties through the different social circles they connect within a network.

concepts.label: Structural holes
concepts.learning_takeaway: Identify brokerage opportunities where otherwise disconnected groups hold different information.
concepts.card: Structural holes are gaps between otherwise disconnected social groups. A person spanning such a gap can encounter contrasting ideas and broker information between groups. Burt’s account focuses on the network position that makes combining perspectives possible when opinion and behavior are more similar within groups than between them.

evidence.locator: Abstract and opening argument, original pp.349–350
evidence.note: Contrasts within-group similarity and between-group differences and states the brokerage/synthesis mechanism.

relations.note: The paper defines brokerage across gaps between groups as a structural property of social networks.

concepts.label: Reference groups
concepts.learning_takeaway: Separate groups used as comparison standards from groups a person actually belongs to.
concepts.card: A reference group provides a standard people use to judge their behavior or aspirations. It need not be a group they belong to: admired athletes can serve as a comparison point. Several reference groups may send competing messages, making apparent personal preferences partly a matter of social comparison.

evidence.note: Defines comparison standards, athlete examples, multiple groups, and conflicting messages.

relations.note: The sociology chapter treats reference groups as sources of standards and norms used in social comparison.

concepts.label: Bass guitar
concepts.learning_takeaway: Hear how identical pitches differ when played on different strings and frets.
concepts.card: A bass guitar can produce the same pitch at different places on its strings. In standard tuning, low A is available as an open A string or at the E string’s fifth fret. Choosing between them changes the sound’s color as well as the fingering.
concepts.original_description: electric or acoustic bass instrument

evidence.note: Gives the exact two low-A locations and explains audible differences between string positions.

relations.note: Comparing an open A with the same pitch fretted on the E string offers an ear-training exercise in timbre while holding pitch constant.

imported_records.description: electric or acoustic bass instrument
imported_records.subsection: Arts and recreation / Music / Musical instruments

concepts.label: Sociology
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect interaction-level observations to wider social patterns.
concepts.card: Sociology studies how people live together, from small interactions to large institutions. A small-scale study might compare conversation rules among teenagers and business professionals. A larger-scale study could follow changes in language use over time, connecting everyday interaction with broader social patterns.
concepts.original_description: social science that studies human society and its development

evidence.locator: What Are Society and Culture?; Studying Patterns
evidence.note: Defines micro and macro sociology and uses accepted conversation rules as an example.

relations.note: Conflicting expectations for an employee and a parent give a concrete case of how social roles shape an individual’s choices.

imported_records.description: social science that studies human society and its development
imported_records.subsection: Society and social sciences / Society / Sociology

concepts.label: Economics
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect scarce resources with specialization and exchange.
