concepts.card: Economics examines choices when time, materials, and other resources are limited. Specialization offers a concrete example: people divide production into different tasks, then depend on exchange to obtain what others make. The field connects those everyday decisions with how households, businesses, and societies organize resources.
concepts.original_description: social science that studies the production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services

evidence.locator: Opening definition; Division of Labor; Specialization and Trade
evidence.note: Defines scarcity-driven choice and explains specialization, division of labor, and exchange.

relations.note: Exchange depends partly on what each side knows; unequal information is a specific complication of the market coordination described by this broad card.

imported_records.description: social science that studies the production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services
imported_records.subsection: Society and social sciences / Business and economics

concepts.label: Confirmation bias
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize belief-consistent selection of evidence and compare an equivalent registered sense.
concepts.card: Confirmation bias favors information that fits an existing belief. If someone expects a teacher to be unfriendly, rude moments may stand out while pleasant encounters receive less attention. That uneven selection can strengthen an impression without giving supporting and challenging observations comparable weight.
concepts.original_description: Examining the tendency to favor information that supports existing beliefs.

evidence.locator: Pitfalls to Problem Solving, confirmation-bias paragraph; Table 7.3
evidence.note: Definition and professor example support biased attention to confirming evidence.

relations.note: Selective attention to evidence affects how beliefs are maintained and revised, a specific cognitive process linking this bias to cognitive psychology.

imported_records.description: Examining the tendency to favor information that supports existing beliefs.

concepts.label: Counterpoint
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish interacting simultaneous melodies from melody with accompaniment.
concepts.card: Counterpoint combines melodic lines that sound at the same time. Each line contributes to the whole, rather than simply acting as accompaniment to one main tune. Species exercises simplify their rhythmic relationships, allowing a composer to focus on how separate melodies fit together.
concepts.original_description: compositional technique based on the combination of several overlapping melodic lines

evidence.locator: §30.1, counterpoint definition, species exercises, and homophonic contrast
evidence.note: Defines simultaneous melodic lines and contrasts contrapuntal with melody-accompaniment textures.

relations.note: Coordinating melodic lines requires analysis of their simultaneous pitch and rhythmic relationships, making counterpoint a specific compositional subject within music theory.

imported_records.description: compositional technique based on the combination of several overlapping melodic lines

concepts.label: Commons governance
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand user-made rules, monitoring, and graduated sanctions as governance mechanisms.
concepts.card: Commons governance concerns the rules people use to manage shared resources. Ostrom’s studies identified recurring features of long-lasting arrangements, including user participation, monitoring, and sanctions that grow with repeated violations. These patterns guide comparison, while actual rules still need to fit local social and environmental conditions.
concepts.original_description: Managing shared resources through collectively developed rules and institutions.

evidence.note: Lists participation, monitoring, graduated sanctions, and congruence with local conditions while distinguishing principles from universal specific rules.

relations.note: Ostrom’s lecture directly describes her comparison of successful and failed commons institutions and the resulting design principles.

imported_records.description: Managing shared resources through collectively developed rules and institutions.

concepts.label: En passant
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand the immediate timing and board conditions of this exceptional pawn capture.
concepts.card: En passant lets a chess pawn capture an opposing pawn immediately after that pawn advances two squares from its starting square. The capturing pawn must be beside it on the same rank and takes it as though it advanced only one square. Waiting loses the opportunity.

evidence.note: The rule states adjacent-file/same-rank geometry, initial two-square advance, as-if-one-square capture, and immediate timing.

relations.note: FIDE places this exception within the pawn-movement rules: the opposing pawn is captured on the square passed over.

concepts.label: Elinor Ostrom
concepts.learning_takeaway: Study Ostrom’s rejection of a single institutional solution through diverse commons cases.
concepts.card: Elinor Ostrom studied how communities and other institutions govern shared resources. Her work compared successful and failed arrangements instead of assuming one universal solution. Monitoring, participation in rule changes, and rules suited to local conditions help explain why institutional design matters for forests, fisheries, and irrigation.

evidence.note: The lecture describes institutional diversity, successful/failed cases, user participation, monitoring, local fit, and resource-user examples.

relations.note: Ostrom explicitly analyzes common-pool-resource institutions and identifies recurring design principles, making her work a documented route into commons governance.

candidate.label: Varve

These patterns guide comparison, while actual rules still need to fit local social and environmental conditions.
findings: Kept recurring features rather than guarantees; avoided treating every successful commons as using an identical institutional recipe.

relation_references_inspected.locator: Introduction, pp.408–409; §4E Long-Surviving Resource Institutions, pp.421–423

reviews.reviewed_card: En passant lets a chess pawn capture an opposing pawn immediately after that pawn advances two squares from its starting square. The capturing pawn must be beside it on the same rank and takes it as though it advanced only one square. Waiting loses the opportunity.
findings: Verified the 2023 numbering and timing; retained existing Q205730 with empty imported records and incremented the prior candidate card version.

relation_references_inspected.locator: Articles 3.7.3.1–2, 9.2–9.6; Guidelines II.3; PDF pp.20,39–40,57–58

reviews.reviewed_card: Elinor Ostrom studied how communities and other institutions govern shared resources. Her work compared successful and failed arrangements instead of assuming one universal solution. Monitoring, participation in rule changes, and rules suited to local conditions help explain why institutional design matters for forests, fisheries, and irrigation.
findings: Used the researcher’s own lecture for the substantive claims; no biography or prize claim was needed to make the named subject informative.

relation_references_inspected.locator: Introduction, pp.408–409; §4E Long-Surviving Resource Institutions, pp.421–423

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Allophone
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Distinguish noncontrastive pronunciations of one phoneme from meaning-changing sound contrasts.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: An allophone is one pronunciation variant within a phoneme, the sound category a language treats as a unit. English speakers can produce voiced and devoiced versions of l without changing a word’s identity. Many such variants are predictable from nearby sounds; others vary more freely.

evidence.locator: Opening definition; Video Script: noncontrastive variants and distribution
evidence.note: Noncontrastive l variants; conditioned distribution and free variation.

relations.note: Phonology investigates how a language organizes noncontrastive sound variants and their environments.
An allophone is a realization grouped within a phoneme; the distinction separates concrete variants from the sound category.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Constructive vote of no confidence
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Understand replacing a head of government by agreeing on a successor in the same parliamentary procedure.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: A constructive vote of no confidence removes a head of government only by agreeing on a replacement. In Germany, the Bundestag must elect a successor rather than merely reject the chancellor. A majority against the incumbent therefore does not suffice without a majority for another candidate.

evidence.note: The Bundestag glossary requires agreement on a new government head and a majority-supported successor.

relations.note: The Bundestag describes this as a parliamentary control mechanism that replaces the chancellor through election of a successor.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Overhang seats
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Understand the extra seats created when constituency victories exceed a party’s proportional entitlement.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: An overhang arises when a party wins more constituency seats than its proportional vote share would normally provide. Under New Zealand’s 2023 allocation rules, it keeps those extra seats, enlarging Parliament. Other parties retain their allocations, so constituency results can alter the legislature’s final size.

evidence.note: Explains excess electorate wins, no additional list seats, increased size, and unchanged other-party allocations.

relations.note: Mixed constituency-and-list representation can generate a mismatch between local victories and proportional entitlement; overhang rules resolve that electoral design problem.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Encoding specificity principle
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Explain why a cue works through overlap with how an event was encoded.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: A memory cue works partly by matching information encoded with the original experience. A song can bring back a particular conversation because both were linked at the time. Encoding specificity explains why the effectiveness of a reminder depends on how the event was originally remembered.

evidence.note: The song/party/conversation example and overlap-with-encoding principle support the explanation.

relations.note: The memory chapter states this principle as an account of which retrieval cues evoke a stored experience.

Both concern encoding–retrieval compatibility. The navigation comparison separates cue–trace information overlap from matching the cognitive operations performed during study and test; it does not claim the theories are wholly independent.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Mutable default arguments in Python
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Explain why mutations to a default list can persist across function calls, and why a None sentinel changes that behavior.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: Python evaluates a function’s default arguments when the definition executes, not on every call. If a default list is mutated, later calls can see the accumulated contents. Using None as the default and creating a list inside the function avoids sharing that default list.

evidence.note: Definition-time evaluation, shared mutable object and fresh-list alternative.

relations.note: Default-argument evaluation is a language-specific function-definition rule whose shared mutable values affect later Python calls.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Swim-bladder buoyancy regulation
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Relate a bony fish’s gas-filled swim bladder and gas exchange with blood to buoyancy control.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: A swim bladder is a gas-filled pouch that helps many bony fishes regulate buoyancy. Its gases often exchange directly with the blood. Adjusting this gas changes support in water, a different job from extracting oxygen through the gills.

evidence.note: The bony-fish passage describes a gas-filled gut-derived pouch controlling buoyancy, frequent blood gas exchange, and separate gill breathing.

relations.note: Editorial placement: the gas-filled swim bladder illustrates how the form and connections of an internal organ enable buoyancy regulation.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Ekphrasis
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: See how writing can interpret or animate visual art instead of merely describing it.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: Ekphrasis uses language to describe or respond to visual art. A poem can do more than list what a painting contains: it may question the image, imagine a figure speaking, or reflect on viewing it. The artwork becomes a starting point for interpretation as well as description.

evidence.note: Visual-art response; interpretation, imagined speech and reflection beyond description.

relations.note: Ekphrastic writing is a specific poetic practice in which a visual work becomes the subject of verbal description or interpretation.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Inclusion–exclusion principle
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Correct double counting by subtracting intersections, with alternating corrections for more sets.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: Adding the sizes of overlapping finite sets counts shared members more than once. Inclusion–exclusion corrects this: subtract pairwise overlaps, then add triple overlaps back, continuing with alternating signs. For two sets, simply subtract their intersection from the sum of their sizes.

evidence.locator: Counting with Venn Diagrams; Principle of Inclusion/Exclusion
evidence.note: Overlap correction and the two-/three-set pattern.

relations.note: Editorial combinatorics placement: the method counts a union by systematically correcting repeated membership in overlapping finite sets.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Crane (lifting machine)
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Recognize a crane as lifting machinery whose boom configuration and load placement determine its capabilities.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: A crane raises and positions loads using lifting machinery and a supporting structure, often including a boom. Its reach is part of its design: changing the boom configuration changes what it can lift. Rated capacities therefore describe specified conditions rather than unlimited lifting power.

evidence.locator: Moving with load on the hook; Multifunctional boom systems; Precise crane control
evidence.note: A crane’s hook, lifting machinery and configurable boom.
Capacity depends on specified configuration and operating radius.

relations.note: Editorial mechanical-engineering placement: hoisting mechanisms and load-support geometry jointly determine a crane’s reach and capacity.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Landscape Evolution Observatory
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: See why replicated artificial hillslopes let researchers measure coupled soil, water and biological changes under controlled conditions.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: The Landscape Evolution Observatory at Biosphere 2 uses three replicated artificial hillslopes filled with crushed basalt. Dense sensor networks follow water, carbon, and energy flows as the landscapes develop. Controlled rainfall and climate allow researchers to test interactions that are difficult to isolate outdoors.

evidence.note: The official description specifies three replicated crushed-basalt slopes, extensive sensors and climate/rainfall control for coupled landscape research.

relations.note: LEO is an Earth-science experiment whose controlled replicated hillslopes measure coupled water, substrate and biological changes.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Blossom-end rot
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Explain why calcium shortage inside developing tomato fruit need not indicate calcium-poor soil.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: Blossom-end rot produces a dark, flattened patch at a tomato’s blossom end when developing fruit lacks enough calcium. The soil may still contain plenty. Fluctuating moisture, root injury, and rapid growth can disrupt delivery, so adding calcium alone need not address the cause.

evidence.note: The disorder has dark flattened fruit-end lesions; calcium shortage in fruit can result from water, root and growth conditions despite soil calcium.

relations.note: Editorial gardening bridge: tomato-fruit damage may reflect disrupted calcium delivery from uneven water or injured roots, shaping cultivation choices.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Mihrab
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a prayer-direction niche from the direction it indicates, and see its ornamental role.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: A mihrab is a niche indicating the direction of Mecca in a mosque or religious school. It gives prayer an architectural focus and can also carry elaborate ornament. The Met’s fourteenth-century Iranian example combines a recessed niche with cut-tile mosaics and religious inscriptions.

evidence.note: Prayer-direction niche; fourteenth-century Iranian tilework and inscriptions.

relations.note: The niche organizes sacred space around prayer direction while its ornament makes that directional focus visually prominent.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Role conflict
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Distinguish incompatible demands across different social roles from pressure within one role.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: Role conflict occurs when expectations attached to different social roles clash. A person’s responsibilities as an employee may demand staying late while responsibilities as a parent require leaving. The problem comes from incompatible roles, even when either role alone would be manageable.

evidence.note: The employee/parent example distinguishes contradictory roles from demands within one role.

relations.note: The sociology chapter locates role conflict in the expected behavior associated with multiple social statuses.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Melodic inversion
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Distinguish reversing melodic interval direction from changing note order.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: Melodic inversion reverses the direction of a tune’s intervals, turning upward motion downward and vice versa. A real inversion preserves exact interval qualities; a tonal inversion adjusts them to stay within a key. The distinction explains how a recognizable mirrored shape can retain different pitch details.

evidence.note: Defines inversion and distinguishes real interval-quality preservation from tonal adaptation to scale or key.

relations.note: The source explicitly presents inversion as one method of altering a melody while relating it to its original motive.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Rain shadow
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Trace orographic rain loss and leeward warming to contrasting vegetation on opposite mountain slopes.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: Mountains can divide wet landscapes from dry ones. Rising air cools and loses moisture as precipitation on windward slopes; descending air warms and dries on the leeward side. Hawaii’s contrasting green and brown slopes make this rain-shadow mechanism visible in vegetation.

evidence.note: The Hawaii account explains windward cooling/precipitation, leeward warming/drying and the corresponding green/brown vegetation pattern.

relations.note: Editorial climatic bridge: mountain-forced ascent and descent repeatedly redistribute moisture, shaping wet and dry sides of a regional landscape.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: PostgreSQL Repeatable Read snapshots
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Understand a transaction’s consistent snapshot and why that guarantee alone is weaker than serial execution.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: PostgreSQL’s Repeatable Read uses a snapshot fixed at the first non-transaction-control statement. Later queries see that snapshot plus their transaction’s own writes, hiding other transactions’ later commits. However, serialization anomalies remain possible: a consistent snapshot alone does not guarantee a one-at-a-time execution history.

evidence.locator: §13.2.2, snapshot timing, own-write exception and serialization warning
evidence.note: PostgreSQL-specific snapshot semantics and remaining anomaly class.

relations.note: This database transaction isolation rule determines which committed row versions are visible during successive reads.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Universal Transverse Mercator grid
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Recognize zone-based planar coordinates as an alternative position notation, not inherently greater accuracy.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: The Universal Transverse Mercator system locates points within sixty zones, normally six degrees of longitude wide. Its plane-coordinate grids offer an alternative to latitude and longitude. Choosing UTM can make certain maps easier to use, but the notation is not inherently more accurate than geographic coordinates.

evidence.note: Sixty-zone plane grid and no inherent accuracy advantage over latitude/longitude.

relations.note: UTM supplies a zone-based plane coordinate framework that cartographers can place on maps to identify locations.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Etching (printmaking)
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Follow how acid converts lines drawn through a protective ground into printable grooves.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: Etching lets acid do the cutting. An artist scratches a design through an acid-resistant coating on a metal plate; acid then bites the exposed lines. Longer exposure deepens them. After the coating is removed, those incisions provide the image for an intaglio print.

evidence.note: Ground, needle exposure, acid biting, depth and intaglio printing.

relations.note: Etching produces an intaglio printing matrix by chemically biting exposed areas of a coated metal plate.
Both form metal-plate incisions, but the source contrasts etching’s acid action with engraving’s direct burin cutting.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Attentional blink
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a temporary second-target reporting deficit from literal blinking.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: The attentional blink is a brief difficulty detecting a second target after identifying a first one in a rapid visual stream. In the original letter experiment, detection fell during a window beginning 180 milliseconds after the target. Ignoring the first target removed that pattern.

evidence.note: Reports the rapid serial letter task, onset of the impaired interval, and absence when first-target identification is not required.

relations.note: The paper manipulates allocation of visual attention between rapidly presented targets and measures the resulting detection deficit.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Geoid
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Understand the idealized gravity-shaped sea surface used as a reference for elevation.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: The geoid models the sea surface after removing tides and currents, extended mathematically through the continents. Its gentle irregularities reflect Earth’s uneven gravitational field. Surveyors use this reference surface when determining elevations, so “height above sea level” involves a physical model rather than a perfectly smooth globe.

evidence.locator: Main explanation of idealized sea surface and elevations
evidence.note: Idealized sea surface, gravity variations, continental extension and elevations.

relations.note: Geodesy uses gravity observations and the geoid model to supply a physical reference for measuring elevations.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Bass (fish)
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Recognize bass as a shared fish common name rather than a single species or family.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: Bass is a common name shared by freshwater and marine fishes, rather than one biological family. Largemouth and smallmouth bass belong to the sunfish family, while striped bass belongs to the temperate bass family. Common names can therefore hide substantial differences in classification.

evidence.note: Lead and Common types establish a shared fish name across freshwater/marine species and distinguish sunfish-family black bass from temperate-family striped bass.

relations.note: The bass common name refers to several fish groups, including sunfishes and temperate basses, without defining one family.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Crane (bird)
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Identify the Gruidae bird family and its extended-neck flight and coordinated communication.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: Cranes are long-legged, long-necked birds of the family Gruidae. Unlike herons, they fly with their necks extended. Their vocal communication includes coordinated pair calls, showing how a familiar silhouette and a distinctive sound can help identify the intended bird group.

evidence.locator: Lead, lines 228–232; Calls and communication, lines 320–324
evidence.note: Lead identifies Gruidae and extended-neck flight; Calls and communication documents pair duets. The identification suggestion is editorial.

relations.note: Cranes form the bird family Gruidae; flight posture and pair calls supply concrete family-level identification cues.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Bass guitar
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Hear how identical pitches differ when played on different strings and frets.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: A bass guitar can produce the same pitch at different places on its strings. In standard tuning, low A is available as an open A string or at the E string’s fifth fret. Choosing between them changes the sound’s color as well as the fingering.

evidence.note: Gives the exact two low-A locations and explains audible differences between string positions.

relations.note: Comparing an open A with the same pitch fretted on the E string offers an ear-training exercise in timbre while holding pitch constant.

imported_records.description: electric or acoustic bass instrument
imported_records.subsection: Arts and recreation / Music / Musical instruments

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Java (programming language)
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Distinguish compiled bytecode from source text and the virtual machine that executes it.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: Java is a programming language whose source code can be compiled into bytecode and executed by a Java virtual machine. The development tools separate writing, compilation, and execution, although source-file launching can combine the last two steps for a small program.

evidence.locator: The Compilation and Execution Cycle in Java; troubleshooting Java VM
evidence.note: Bytecode workflow, virtual-machine execution and source-file launching.

relations.note: The Java workflow explicitly uses a compiler to translate source text into bytecode before virtual-machine execution.

imported_records.description: An object-oriented programming language.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Java (island)
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Recognize the Indonesian island’s volcanic spine without confusing its name with a programming language.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: Java, the Indonesian island, has an east–west chain of volcanic mountains running through its interior. It is also home to several major languages, including Javanese and Sundanese. Studying the island therefore involves both a distinctive physical landscape and linguistic differences within one geographic place.

evidence.locator: Disambiguation note; lead paragraphs on volcanic spine and languages
evidence.note: Island identity, volcanic spine and major languages.

relations.note: Java’s volcanic mountain chain offers a specific case for studying how physical landforms organize an island’s landscape.
The presence of Javanese, Sundanese and other languages makes Java a geographic case for examining multilingual societies.

imported_records.description: An island of Indonesia.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Raoult’s law
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Relate each component’s partial vapor pressure to its mole fraction in an ideal solution.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: For an ideal solution, Raoult’s law gives each component’s vapor pressure contribution as its liquid mole fraction times its pure vapor pressure at the same temperature. Adding a nonvolatile solute therefore lowers the solvent’s contribution, connecting mixture composition with the vapor above it.

evidence.locator: Vapor Pressure Lowering, Raoult’s law definition and equation
evidence.note: Ideal-mixture proportionality and nonvolatile-solute consequence.

relations.note: The law specifies component vapor pressures above an ideal solution, so it is a property of solution composition and equilibrium.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Choked flow
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Recognize the ideal gas-flow limit at a sonic throat for fixed upstream total conditions and area.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: For steady gas flow without heat transfer or friction, mass flow is limited when the nozzle throat becomes sonic. With throat area and upstream total pressure and temperature fixed, this choking limits throughput. Gas may still accelerate supersonically farther downstream.

evidence.locator: Mass-flow maximum, equations 10–19 and sonic throat
evidence.note: Fixed-area and fixed-total-state sonic mass-flow limit.

evidence.locator: Sonic throat and supersonic downstream expansion
evidence.note: Choking does not prohibit downstream supersonic flow.

relations.note: Editorial aerodynamic placement: compressibility links gas density and velocity, producing a sonic mass-flow maximum for fixed total conditions.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Skin pigmentation and pulse oximetry
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Explain why an optical oxygen estimate can have skin-pigmentation-dependent error and cannot be treated as an infallible reading.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: A pulse oximeter estimates blood oxygen saturation using light. Skin pigmentation can affect its accuracy, and the FDA highlights concerns about poorer performance in darker skin. Circulation, skin temperature, and nail polish can also alter readings, making the displayed number an estimate with limitations.

evidence.locator: Opening explanation; FDA Efforts; February 2021 Safety Communication, lines 83, 97–131
evidence.note: The page explains optical oxygen estimates, FDA concern about darker-skin accuracy, and circulation, temperature and nail-polish effects.

relations.note: Editorial clinical bridge: interpreting an optical oxygen measurement requires accounting for pigmentation and other sources of device error.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Sodium–glucose cotransport in oral rehydration
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Explain why glucose and sodium together promote intestinal water absorption during diarrhea.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: Oral rehydration exploits coupled absorption of sodium and glucose in the intestine; water follows the resulting osmotic gradient. This transport pathway can keep working during severe diarrhea. More concentrated mixtures are not automatically better, because excessive solute concentration can impair net water absorption.

evidence.locator: Scientific Basis for Oral Rehydration Therapy, lines 46–49
evidence.note: The transport discussion supports sodium–glucose coupling, passive osmotic water movement, preserved function in diarrhea, and problems from high osmolarity.

relations.note: Editorial clinical bridge: formulated oral rehydration uses preserved intestinal sodium–glucose transport to restore fluid absorption during diarrheal illness.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Fiber saturation point in wood
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Distinguish water bound in cell walls from free cavity water and locate the practical onset of moisture-sensitive wood properties.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: Wood contains water in cell cavities and within cell walls. The fiber saturation point describes walls saturated with bound water after free cavity water is gone. Below this approximate boundary, losing wall-bound water changes dimensions; its measured value varies with wood and method.

evidence.locator: Fiber Saturation, pp. 4–2 to 4–3; Dimensional Stability, p. 4–7
evidence.note: The fiber-saturation discussion defines bound versus free water, identifies dimensional change below the boundary, and qualifies specimen/method variation.

relations.note: The fiber-saturation boundary concerns water in wood cell walls versus cavities and marks a practical change in moisture-dependent properties.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Archimedes Palimpsest
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Understand how reuse of parchment preserved older mathematical texts underneath a prayer book.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: The Archimedes Palimpsest is a medieval Greek prayer book made from reused parchment. Earlier writing was scraped away, and leaves were turned and folded again. Beneath the prayers survive mathematical texts, including Archimedes’ otherwise lost Method of Mechanical Theorems, showing how material reuse can preserve knowledge.

evidence.locator: The Book’s Contents; How Was it Made?
evidence.note: Reused parchment, rotated leaves, prayer text and surviving Method.

relations.note: Because this manuscript preserves an otherwise lost Archimedean treatise, it offers a material case for studying how historians recover ancient mathematics.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Fire alteration of obsidian hydration evidence
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Recognize that heating can invalidate a dating surface without requiring complete artifact destruction.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: An obsidian tool can survive a fire while losing useful dating evidence. Heating may alter its surface enough to invalidate obsidian hydration dating. The problem separates two kinds of preservation: a recognizable artifact can remain even after the surface information needed for dating has changed.

evidence.locator: Wildfire impacts, paragraph beginning Wildland fires can impact archeological resources
evidence.note: Wildfire heat can alter a surface so hydration dating is unusable.

relations.note: Fire-related surface alteration is a documented limitation on using obsidian hydration to infer an artifact’s age.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Projex
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Connect winning loops in a projective-plane game to the topology of its board.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: Projex is a connection game played on a representation of the real projective plane. Players color tiles to form a loop that cannot shrink to a point on that surface. Its spherical display pairs opposite tiles, making an abstract topological identification part of every move.

evidence.note: Defines Projective Hex, noncontractible winning cycles, the antipodal sphere representation, and paired coloring.

relations.note: Players alternately occupy a defined board to meet a connection objective; this makes the named topological game a concrete board-game example.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: The Market for Lemons
aliases: The Market for Lemons: Quality Uncertainty and the Market Mechanism
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Read Akerlof’s used-car model as a mechanism by which hidden quality can drive good products out of trade.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: George Akerlof’s 1970 paper The Market for Lemons uses used cars to model hidden quality. If buyers cannot distinguish good cars from bad ones, the price they offer can discourage owners of good cars from selling, worsening the quality available for trade.

evidence.locator: Original pp.488–489, Introduction and II.A; PDF pp.2–3
evidence.note: Title, authorship, year, illustrative automobile market, asymmetric knowledge, and withdrawal of good cars are established on the inspected pages.

relations.note: Akerlof explicitly models sellers knowing car quality better than buyers and shows how this asymmetric information affects which cars trade.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Doctrine of double effect
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Separate intending harm as a means from foreseeing it as a side effect while retaining proportionality constraints.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: The doctrine of double effect distinguishes harm intended as a means from harm foreseen as a side effect. It argues that the latter may sometimes be permissible when the former is not. Proportionality and other conditions matter; merely calling harm unintended does not automatically justify it.

evidence.note: The doctrine’s intended-means/foreseen-side-effect distinction and cumulative conditions are explicit.

relations.note: The entry presents double effect as a principle for judging the moral permissibility of actions with good and harmful effects.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Eruv (carrying enclosure)
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Understand how a valid enclosure and shared food permit carrying within a joined Shabbat domain.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: An eruv is a Jewish legal arrangement that permits carrying within a joined domain on Shabbat. It combines a valid enclosure with shared food that unites the residents. The boundaries follow religious-law requirements rather than property ownership, making activities such as taking a stroller outside possible.

evidence.locator: Definition; valid enclosure; shared food; uses
evidence.note: Valid enclosure, shared food, domain rules and carrying/stroller example.

relations.note: The eruv operates within Jewish Shabbat carrying rules by joining enclosed spaces and their residents into one domain.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Chemistry
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Connect visible material behavior with molecular explanations and symbolic formulas.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: Chemistry studies substances and their changes at several connected scales. Water boiling is directly observable; attractions between water molecules help explain it; the formula H2O represents the substance symbolically. Moving between observations, molecular models, and symbols is central to interpreting chemical experiments.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Parker Solar Probe
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Distinguish hot sparse plasma from heat transfer and identify the role of the probe’s radiation shield.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: Parker Solar Probe shows why temperature alone does not determine heating. The Sun’s corona is extremely hot but sparse, so relatively few particles transfer energy to the spacecraft. A carbon-composite shield separately protects its body from the Sun’s intense radiation.

evidence.locator: The Science Behind Why It Won’t Melt; The Shield That Protects It
evidence.note: Low particle density versus temperature and carbon-composite radiation shield.

relations.note: Editorial thermal-learning bridge: the probe separates particle temperature, collisional energy transfer and radiative shielding in one engineered case.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Urban heat islands
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Distinguish hot urban surfaces from warmer urban air while linking both with built form and vegetation.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: Urban heat islands involve built-up areas that are warmer than their surroundings. Reduced vegetation limits shade and evaporative cooling, while buildings and pavement store heat. Surface temperatures and air temperatures are different measurements, so a hot roof does not directly describe the air above it.
frozen_card_snapshot.original_description: Studying why built-up areas retain heat and how design can reduce it.

evidence.note: EPA supports vegetation-related shade/moisture cooling, built-surface heat storage, and distinct surface versus atmospheric heat-island measurements.

relations.note: Editorial radiative bridge: the EPA describes reduced solar reflection by common urban materials; albedo formalizes that reflectivity, alongside other heat-island mechanisms.

imported_records.description: Studying why built-up areas retain heat and how design can reduce it.

frozen_card_snapshot.label: Silk Road
frozen_card_snapshot.learning_takeaway: Explain how a trading network also supported movement of religious communities.
frozen_card_snapshot.card: The Silk Road names a network of routes, not one continuous highway. Its connections carried beliefs as well as goods. Buddhist monasteries offered lodging to traveling merchants, while merchants supported monasteries, illustrating a practical relationship between trade infrastructure and the movement of religious communities.

original_relations.note: Phonology investigates how a language organizes noncontrastive sound variants and their environments.

card_reviews.label: Mutable default arguments in Python
card_reviews.original_card_text: Python evaluates a function’s default arguments when the definition executes, not on every call. card_reviews.original_learning_takeaway: Explain why mutations to a default list can persist across function calls, and why a None sentinel changes that behavior.

card_fact_review.note: Definition-time evaluation, mutation persisting across calls and the None-sentinel/new-list alternative are explicitly demonstrated by the Python tutorial. This is a particular language rule rather than a general claim about all default parameters.

card_reviews.label: Inclusion–exclusion principle
card_reviews.original_card_text: Adding the sizes of overlapping finite sets counts shared members more than once. Inclusion–exclusion corrects this: subtract pairwise overlaps, then add triple overlaps back, continuing with alternating signs. For two sets, simply subtract their intersection from the sum of their sizes.
card_reviews.original_learning_takeaway: Correct double counting by subtracting intersections, with alternating corrections for more sets.

original_relations.note: Editorial combinatorics placement: the method counts a union by systematically correcting repeated membership in overlapping finite sets.

access_and_evidence_limits.url_retry_rule: No failed URL request was repeated; all references were available. Cached source-navigation operations locate passages without treating failed lookups or snippets as evidence. Prior EPA and Silk Road views were reused; no URL received more than two initial open attempts across this reviewer’s work.
access_and_evidence_limits.scanned_pdf_handling: The Akerlof PDF exposed cover text only. The reviewer independently read rendered images of original pages 488–489 already cached in the shared workspace; hashes and page locations are recorded. This resolved a text-extraction limitation rather than substituting a snippet or an author’s assurance.
access_and_evidence_limits.phrase_lookup_limitation: The first cached exact-phrase search for real inversion returned no match; reading §11.2.1 displayed the real/tonal definition and resolved the navigation issue.
access_and_evidence_limits.revision_limit: Wikipedia revisions agree with the frozen source records. Other sources can have mutable pages or null immutable revisions; the three added footer dates are explicitly update labels.
access_and_evidence_limits.source_assertion_boundary: Relationships were checked against the actual cited passages. Editorial edges retain that label even when factual premises are sourced. A related_to edge does not establish a prerequisite or equivalence.

audit_boundary: This audit covers all claims and all cited relationship references in the fixed 40-card sample. It is not independent source verification of the other 160 cards.

The sample combines a reproducibly selected 20-new stratum with 20 nonoverlapping purposive risk cards; the combined sample is not a simple random sample and does not provide an overall catalog defect-rate estimate.

Source support is not raw-data replication, a guarantee of every cited source’s underlying conclusions, a historical replay of authors’ reading, or a proof of catalog completeness or curiosity/interest expansion.

Original cards, edges, source metadata and sample membership are preserved. Only the one documented relation correction and three source-update-label enrichments were independently rechecked in the working candidate.

before.note: Ekphrastic writing is a specific poetic practice in which a visual work becomes the subject of verbal description or interpretation.

after.note: Editorial classification: this verbal literary response to visual art belongs within literature; the cited poetic examples show one form rather than an exhaustive parent field.

corrections.reason: The general ekphrasis identity is broader than poetry. The independently inspected definition supports the verbal-to-visual premise; Literature is a verified broader baseline identity and the taxonomy remains editorial.
